title: A graduate student spotted it on paper.
description:
A graduate student spotted it on paper. National Geographic says the first sign was on 6 August 1967, in a squiggly stretch of readout under a quarter inch long, while she was a Cambridge graduate student.

They half joked it was aliens. Britannica says the team jokingly dubbed the regular pulses LGM, for Little Green Men.

The Nobel press release credits Ryle for aperture synthesis and Hewish for his decisive role in the discovery of pulsars. It does not mention Bell Burnell.

Prominent scientists objected. Britannica says several protested her omission, though she maintained the prize was presented appropriately given her student status.

Her 2018 Special Breakthrough Prize. National Geographic says she is donating it to a UK charity supporting physics graduate students from under-represented groups.

She found the pulses. The prize went to her advisor.

Sources:
- https://www.nationalgeographic.com/science/article/news-jocelyn-bell-burnell-breakthrough-prize-pulsars-astronomy: read via fetch agent (21 Nov 2026), 6 September 2018. Established that she was a graduate student at Cambridge in 1967, that the first sign was on 6 August 1967 in a squiggly stretch of paper readout under a quarter inch long, that higher speed recordings in November 1967 showed pulses a bit more than a second apart, and that she was awarded a $3 million Special Breakthrough Prize in Fundamental Physics and is donating it to a UK charity supporting physics graduate students from under-represented groups.
- https://www.britannica.com/biography/Jocelyn-Bell-Burnell: read via fetch agent (21 Nov 2026). Established that the team jokingly dubbed the pulses LGM, for Little Green Men, that the 1974 Nobel Prize in Physics went to Hewish and Martin Ryle, that several prominent scientists protested the omission of Bell Burnell, and that she maintained the prize was presented appropriately given her student status at the time.
- https://www.nobelprize.org/prizes/physics/1974/press-release/: read via fetch agent (21 Nov 2026), press release of 15 October 1974. Established that Ryle and Hewish were awarded the prize, Ryle for his observations and inventions, in particular of the aperture synthesis technique, and Hewish for his decisive role in the discovery of pulsars, with no mention of Bell Burnell.
